Abstract
Patient simulators are gaining traction in mental
health training by providing scalable exposure
to complex and sensitive patient interactions.
Simulating depressed patients is particularly
challenging, as safety constraints and high pa-
tient variability complicate simulations and un-
derscore the need for simulators that capture
diverse and realistic patient behaviors. How-
ever, existing evaluations heavily rely on LLM-
judges with poorly specified prompts and do
not assess behavioral diversity. We introduce
PSI-Bench, an automatic evaluation framework
that provides interpretable, clinically grounded
diagnostics of depression patient simulator be-
havior across turn-, dialogue-, and population-
level dimensions. Using PSI-Bench, we bench-
mark seven LLMs across two simulator frame-
works and find that simulators produce overly
long, lexically diverse responses, show reduced
variability, resolve emotions too quickly, and
follow a uniform negative-to-positive trajectory.
We also show that the simulation framework
has a larger impact on fidelity than the model
scale. Results from a human study demonstrate
that our benchmark is strongly aligned with
expert judgments. Our work reveals key lim-
itations of current depression patient simula-
tors and provides an interpretable, extensible
benchmark to guide future simulator design and
evaluation.

Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly
used to simulate human behavior in interactive set-
tings where real-world practice is costly, sensitive,
or difficult to scale (Park et al., 2023; Yao et al.,
2024; Zhou et al., 2024). In mental health educa-
tion, LLM-based patient simulators can generate
clinically plausible responses and act as stand-ins
for real patients, offering a practical training en-
vironment for novice clinicians (Liu et al., 2025;
Wang et al., 2024; Louie et al., 2024). The fi-
delity of these simulated patients is critical, as di-
vergence from real patient communication, such as
in language use or conversational progression, can
risk reinforcing misconceptions and undermining
training effectiveness (Mehri et al., 2025; Abdul-
hai et al., 2025; Naous et al., 2026). Therefore,
it is essential to evaluate simulator fidelity with
real patient behavior. In this work, we focus on a
particularly challenging domain of mental health:
depression. Simulating depression is difficult be-
cause LLMs’ safety training limits their ability to
mimic depressive speech patterns (Liu et al., 2025)
and because depression varies widely between in-
dividuals (Fried and Nesse, 2015).
Current automatic evaluations of patient simula-
tor fidelity rely on LLM-judges to assess how well
generated responses align with the target patient
profiles (Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024). They
typically score responses on a 5-point Likert scale
(Likert, 1932) using generic prompts, entrusting
the LLM-judge to infer nuanced clinical distinc-
tions without explicit grounding in psychological
theory or real patient data. LLM-judges are not
always reliable evaluators in this setting, as Wang
et al. (2024) reports opposite trends between LLM-
judge fidelity scores and expert ratings. Moreover,
these evaluations lack the interpretability needed to
reveal where a simulator diverges from real patient
behavior, offering little guidance for improving fu-
ture simulators. Additionally, existing evaluation
approaches (Sabour et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024;
Liu et al., 2025) report an average score without
examining whether the simulators reflect the dis-
tributional diversity of real patient populations. In
real clinical settings, patients can exhibit varying
linguistic and interactional patterns (Ruiz-Yu et al.,
2025), especially among depressed patients (Fried
and Nesse, 2015). If simulators fail to reflect such
distributional diversity, they may produce behav-
iorally homogeneous patients and introduce bias in
clinician training (Schwieters et al., 2023).

Recognizing these limitations, we propose
Patient-SImulator-Bench (PSI-BENCH), a frame-
work for interpretable, clinically grounded evalua-
tion of depression simulator across turn-, dialogue-,
and population-level dimensions. PSI-Bench com-
prises five dimensions supported by established
psychological and psycholinguistic research (Rude
et al., 2004; Trifu et al., 2024; O’Dea et al., 2021;
Tølbøll, 2019; Smirnova et al., 2018; Beck, 1967),
ensuring that the evaluation meaningfully captures
the characteristics of depression behavior. Using
a shared set of patient profiles, we evaluate simu-
lated and real responses independently under these
dimensions, and compare the resulting statistics
using distance- and similarity-based measures to
quantify simulator alignment with real patient be-
havior. To evaluate whether PSI-Bench provides
meaningful and reliable diagnostics of depression
simulator behavior, we use PSI-Bench to investi-
gate three research questions:
• RQ1: How do responses generated by current
depression patient simulators differ from real
patients responses across turn-level, dialogue-
level, and population-level?
• RQ2: How do different LLMs and simulation
strategies affect simulator fidelity?
• RQ3: Do the findings for RQ1 and RQ2 using
PSI-Bench align with expert judgments?
We evaluate seven LLMs across two simulation
frameworks (PATIENT-Ψ (Wang et al., 2024) and
Roleplay-doh (Louie et al., 2024)), and reveal key
simulator limitations not captured by previous au-
tomatic evaluation approaches. At the population
level, simulators show less variability and diverge
from real patients in dialogue progression: they
move through therapeutic stages more rapidly and
follow a uniform negative-to-positive emotional
trajectory. They also produce overly long, lexically
diverse responses at the message level, and exhibit
a more spread out presence of depressive markers
at the dialogue level.
We aggregate scores across all dimensions into
a unified alignment score to rank the simulators
(Table 1), while retaining interpretable diagnos-
tics at each level. This allows us to examine how
simulation frameworks, model scale, and model
family influence fidelity. We find that the simu-
lation framework has a larger impact than LLM
capability: PATIENT-Ψ consistently outperforms
Roleplay-doh, and smaller models sometimes sur-
pass larger ones, suggesting that increased linguis-
tic sophistication can reduce behavioral fidelity
to real patient communication. Finally, we val-
idate our benchmark via expert evaluation with
20 mental health experts. The results show near-
perfect agreement with the PSI-Bench rankings
(κ = 0.82), supporting PSI-Bench as a reliable
evaluation framework.
Overall, our work aims to enable future research
towards advancing depression patient simulators
through these main contributions:
• We introduce PSI-Bench, an interpretable, clini-
cally grounded benchmark for evaluating patient
simulators by alignment with real patients, show-
ing strong agreement with expert judgments.
• Using PSI-Bench, we highlight previously un-
derexplored simulator divergences from real
patient behavior and the impact of simulation
framework, scale, and model family on simula-
tor fidelity.

Related Work
2.1
LLM-based Simulators
User Simulators for Dialogue Systems Since the
mid-1990s, user simulators have been widely stud-
ied to address the high cost and difficulty of collect-
ing real conversational data, particularly in special-
ized domains (Pietquin and Hastie, 2013). While
traditional rule-based, statistical, and early neural
approaches struggled to capture the complexity and
naturalness of human behavior, LLMs show poten-
tial in overcoming these challenges with their pow-
erful language capabilities (Naveed et al., 2025).
Existing work mainly explores two applications
of LLM-based simulators. First, they are used to
train and evaluate AI systems, either by generating
large volumes of synthetic dialogue data (Finch
and Choi, 2024; Bao et al., 2023), or by serving as
interactive environments for online reinforcement
learning (Carta et al., 2023). Second, they are used
as training tools for human learners in domains
where practicing with real individuals is costly or
sensitive, such as nurse communication training
(Lee et al., 2025) and counseling (Na et al., 2025).
LLM-based Patient Simulators in Mental
Health Within the counseling domain, several
works (Chen et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024) focus
on the first application – generating counseling
datasets to improve counselor LLMs, where a pa-
tient simulator’s design and evaluation are less pri-
oritized. In contrast, our evaluation framework
targets the second application – simulating patients
for training novice counselors, where the central
emphasis is on designing simulated patients with
realistic behaviors (Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al.,
2024; Louie et al., 2024).
2.2
Evaluation of Patient Simulators
Evaluating User Simulators Before the advent
of LLMs, Pietquin and Hastie (2013) grouped the
evaluation of user simulators into two groups: turn-
level metrics that evaluate individual responses
(e.g., precision and recall) and dialogue-level met-
rics that evaluate general interaction (e.g., task
completion). Though fast and reproducible, these
traditional metrics rely on surface lexical overlap
and miss deeper nuances (Gu et al., 2025). Along
with the rise of LLM-based simulators, LLM-based
evaluation methods emerged with their strong rea-
soning and language capabilities, enabling more
context-aware assessment but also introducing new
systematic bias (Gu et al., 2025; Gallegos et al.,
2024). Evaluation can also be framed as intrinsic
versus extrinsic: intrinsic methods assess simulator
outputs directly (e.g., realism and diversity), while
extrinsic methods measure downstream task impact.
Naous et al. (2026) show that extrinsic evaluation
alone can be misleading as over-cooperative LLM
users may inflate system performance, motivating
greater emphasis on intrinsic methods.
Evaluating LLM-based Patient Simulators in
Counseling Simulation systems aimed at training
or benchmarking counselor LLMs (Lee et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2025) are often automatically evaluated
using extrinsic metrics of counseling effectiveness.
Consistent with the findings of Naous et al. (2026),
such simulated patients can be implicitly coopera-
tive and demonstrate rapid improvement (Abdulhai
et al., 2025), thus increasing these extrinsic perfor-
mance scores.
Patient simulators aimed at training novice coun-
selors are typically evaluated for alignment, real-
ism, and training utility (Liu et al., 2025; Wang
et al., 2024; Louie et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2026).
Expert human evaluation and automatic methods
assess profile alignment and behavioral fidelity,
with experts also judging pedagogical effectiveness.
It is often impractical to use expert evaluation alone
as it is costly and not scalable, while current au-
tomatic evaluation pipelines, which primarily use
LLM-Judge Likert ratings (Wang et al., 2024), have
significant limitations. They are reported to be un-
reliable or even contradict expert judgments (Wang
et al., 2024). Additionally, these automatic eval-
uations typically report an average score without
examining broader behavioral distributions reflect-
ing real-world clinical variability. Our evaluation
framework addresses these limitations.
3
PSI-Bench
Figure 1 provides an overview of PSI-Bench. We
utilize the Eeyore dataset (Liu et al., 2025), de-
rived from public depression-related real dialogue
datasets, where each conversation is paired with
a patient profile describing the situation and traits
(see Appendix A.1). We generate simulated con-
versations by conditioning patient simulators on
these patient profiles, with another LLM as the
therapist to sustain the dialogue. Simulators gener-
ate messages turn by turn using prior context, with
each turn comprising one patient and one therapist
message. Both real and synthetic datasets are then


evaluated independently using PSI-Bench dimen-
sions, and the resulting statistics are compared.
We ground our assessment in behaviors observed
in depression-related communication and analyze
simulator behavior across five interpretable dimen-
sions. Section 3.1 introduces and independently
applies these dimensions to real and synthetic con-
versations. Section 3.2 describes how simulators’
scores are compared relative to real patient scores
at multiple levels: turn-level (e.g., response length),
conversation-level (e.g., progression and emotional
change), and population-level (e.g., diversity across
profiles), capturing realistic patterns and variation
observed in practice. Each dimension is aggregated
into normalized scalar scores for comparison, rank-
ing, and correlation with expert evaluation.
3.1
Evaluation Dimensions
Narrative-Emotion Processes (NEP) Markers
are standardized categories rated by observers that
capture how patients manifest narrative content and
emotional experience during psychotherapy (An-
gus et al., 2017). Because the evolving pattern
of these markers over a session reflects therapeutic
progress, they provide a basis for assessing whether
simulated patients replicate the change dynamics
observed in real clinical conversations. The mark-
ers are grouped into three categories: Problem:
repetitive, “stuck” storylines with limited reflec-
tion; Transition: more coherent and reflective sto-
rytelling as clients begin to examine their thoughts
and emotions; Change: clear shifts in emotional
response and thought patterns, where clients may
show a new understanding of key events in their life.
To track these patterns, we prompt gpt-oss-120b
(OpenAI, 2025) to classify each patient turn in
conversations as Problem, Transition, Change, or
Filler (neutral procedural replies without meaning-
ful therapeutic content), using explicit definitions
and decision criteria (Appendix A.3).
Emotion Expression We examine how simulated
and real patients express emotions over the course
of a conversation. Beck’s cognitive theory of de-
pression posits that depressed individuals have a
negative view of themselves, others, and the future
(Beck, 1967), leading to more negative emotional
expression in conversation. Supporting this, Tøl-
bøll (2019); Rude et al. (2004) show that depression
correlates with increased negative and decreased
positive emotion words. Building on these insights,
we investigate the temporal dynamics of emotional
expression to determine whether simulated and real
patients differ in how their emotions evolve dur-
ing a dialogue. We employ gpt-oss-120b to clas-
sify each patient message into one of Plutchik’s
eight primary emotions (trust, fear, anger, dis-
gust, joy, anticipation, sadness, and surprise) along
with a neutral category. Finally, we analyze the
population-level distributions of these labels as con-
versations progress.
Lexical Diversity Smirnova et al. (2018) showed
that patients with depression often exhibit repe-
tition in words or ideas.
We evaluate whether
simulators can mimic this behavior despite LLMs’
tendency to generate highly diverse text (Li et al.,
2025). We also investigate how lexical diversity
varies across real patients and whether the same
LLM conditioned on different profiles can mirror
such variation. We compute conversation-level lex-
ical diversity by concatenating all patient messages
in a conversation and applying the Measure of
Textual Lexical Diversity (MTLD) (McCarthy and
Jarvis, 2010). MTLD is defined as the mean length
of word sequences required to reach a fixed ratio
(0.72) of unique words to total words (Appendix
A.4). Additionally, we concatenate all patient mes-
sages across profiles into a single corpus and com-
pute its MTLD. A lower corpus-level MTLD than
the average per-conversation MTLD would suggest
some degree of shared vocabulary across patients.
Response Length Patients with depression tend to
produce shorter utterances and more limited con-
tent in conversation (Trifu et al., 2024; Smirnova
et al., 2018), while LLMs tend to be more verbose
(Li et al., 2025). We assess response length by com-
puting average number of words per message and
average number of words per sentence.
Linguistic Markers of Depression Psychologi-
cal research identifies consistent linguistic patterns
in depressed patients that correlate with increased
use of: (1) absolutist terms: words denoting to-
tality of magnitude or probability, reflecting abso-
lutist thinking underlying many cognitive distor-
tions (e.g. "always", "never") (Al-Mosaiwi and
Johnstone, 2018), (2) depressive words associated
with low mood and hopelessness (Li et al., 2020),
and (3) non-fluencies: hesitations and fillers that
may signal cognitive or emotional strain (O’Dea
et al., 2021). The complete lexicon used in our anal-
ysis is provided in Table 7. These marker categories

Simulation Strategies

or the number of patient turns in the correspond-
ing real conversation, whichever is smaller. Our
experiment spans 14 dataset configurations across
framework–LLM pairings.

4.2
Human study design
To assess the reliability of our metrics and answer
RQ3, we conducted a human evaluation study via
Prolific with 20 mental health experts, divided into
four groups (5 annotators per group), each eval-
uating conversations from a different set of three
patient profiles. For each profile, annotators per-
formed two tasks: (1) message-level classification,
labeling each patient message by its primary emo-
tion and narrative-emotion process, to evaluate the
reliability of our LLM-based classifications; (2)
pairwise comparison, selecting which of two sim-
ulated conversation snippets better reflects how a
real patient would communicate, to assess agree-
ment with our benchmark rankings. More details
(annotation interface, annotator demographics, etc.)
are provided in Appendix B.
From our PSI-Bench benchmark rankings, we
randomly sample conversation pairs from simula-
tors with a minimum ranking difference of four.
We evaluate alignment by whether experts consis-
tently prefer outputs from higher-ranked simula-
tors. For both tasks, we use majority voting within
each group to determine the final human annota-

5
Results
5.1
RQ1: Divergence from Real patients
Comparing real and synthetic conversations across
our evaluation dimensions reveals clear diver-
gences in simulator behavior from real patients. We
summarize the key findings below, with detailed
results in Appendix C.
Premature resolution of emotional narratives
Figure 2a displays the progression of population-
level distributions of NEP markers across dialogue
turns. This figure shows that simulated patients
progress through narrative–emotion stages much
faster than humans.
Although all populations
mostly start the conversation in the problem stage,
real patients transition gradually, with over 40%
remaining in this stage throughout the first 16 turns.
In contrast, simulators quickly shift away from
problem by around turn 3, with rapid percentage in-
creases in transition and change. This suggests pre-
mature narrative resolution and greater emotional
awareness than real patients, who typically require
longer interaction to make therapeutic progress.

5.3
RQ3: Correlation with Expert judgements
Table 2 reports agreement between expert judg-
ments and our benchmark rankings and LLM-based
classifications. Following the interpretation of Lan-
dis and Koch (1977), inter-annotator agreement is
moderate across tasks (Fleiss’ κ between 0.43 and
0.57). However, agreements between our methods
and expert majority labels are high: pairwise pref-
erence shows almost perfect alignment (κ = 0.82),
while NEP marker and emotion classification show
substantial agreement (κ = 0.7 and 0.75, respec-
tively). These results confirm that PSI-Bench pro-
vides reliable and expert-aligned evaluations.
Expert annotators’ qualitative feedback corrobo-
rates our findings in Section 5.1 on divergences be-
tween simulated and real patient behavior. Less re-
alistic conversations were described as overly struc-
tured, polished, and cognitively organized. They re-
semble a “coherent story” rather than spontaneous
distress, often featuring sophisticated vocabulary
and lacking hesitation or disfluency. Annotators
also noted that simulated patients are excessively
self-reflective and articulate, which was consid-
ered implausible in early interactions where real
patients tend to struggle with articulation. Addition-
ally, simulated responses were often prematurely
solution-oriented, proposing coping strategies or ra-
tional interpretations, unlike real patients who may
initially feel overwhelmed or cognitively blocked.
While annotators more often justified their
choices by critiquing the less realistic option, some
identified reasons certain conversations appeared
more realistic. These were described as shorter,
less certain, and more fragmented, using simpler
language and exhibiting hesitation, self-correction,
and slightly disjointed thought patterns. Notably,
these conversations largely came from our top-
ranked settings. In one instance, an annotator re-
marked that a conversation from our top-1 setting
“seems most human and the realest of all the conver-
sations in this block” (Table 10). These feedback
further provide qualitative support for PSI-Bench’s
alignment with expert judgments.
6
Conclusion
We introduce PSI-Bench, an interpretable and
clinically grounded evaluation framework that de-
composes simulator behavior into psychologically
meaningful dimensions and evaluates alignment
with real patient conversations. Empirical analysis
reveals underexplored divergences between sim-
ulated and real patients, showing that simulators
are less varied, transition through therapeutic states
more quickly, follow a stereotyped emotional tra-
jectory, and produce overly verbose, lexically rich
responses compared to real patients. Across con-
figurations, we find that the simulation framework
plays a more critical role than the LLM model.
Importantly, PSI-Bench demonstrates strong align-
ment with expert judgments, both quantitatively
and qualitatively, supporting its validity as a reli-
able automatic evaluation framework. We hope
PSI-Bench can facilitate future research towards
advancing depression patient simulators.

A.4
MTLD Formulation
We use the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity
(MTLD) (McCarthy and Jarvis, 2010), defined as
the mean length of word sequences required to
reach a fixed type–token ratio (TTR) threshold
of 0.72, where TTR is number of different words
(type) divided by total number of words (token).
A major limitation of traditional lexical diversity
indices is their sensitivity to text length – after
reaching a point of stabilization, TTR tends to
monotonically decrease as the number of tokens


increases (McCarthy and Jarvis, 2010). MTLD mit-
igates this issue by measuring how many tokens,
on average, are required to reach this stabilization
point. Each time the TTR threshold is reached, a
factor count F is incremented and TTR computa-
tion is reset for subsequent tokens. Lexical diver-
sity is then estimated as the ratio of the total number
of words N to F, computed separately for forward
(Ffwd) and backward (Fbwd) passes through the text.
The final MTLD score is obtained by averaging
these two estimates, which has been shown to yield
more stable measurements.

Human Study Details
The Human Study procedure was reviewed by the
Institutional Review Board (IRB) and determined
not to meet the definition of Human Subjects Re-
search.
Participants.
We recruited 20 annotators from
Prolific, assigned into four groups of five. Eligibil-
ity was restricted to individuals fluent in English
and with current job roles in mental health or re-
lated care professions, including clinical psycholo-
gist, psychologist, counsellor (mental health), occu-
pational therapist, and social worker. Participants
were compensated at a rate of $15/hour. Table 8
shows anonymized demographic statistics of these
20 annotators.
Classification Task.
In the message-level clas-
sification task, the annotators labeled each patient
message with one label dominant emotion and one
narrative-emotion process. Annotators were in-
structed to classify patient turns only; therapist
messages were shown only as context. Figure 7
shows the classification interface.
For dominant emotion, annotators selected one
label from the following options: anger, disgust,
fear, joy, sadness, surprise, anticipation, trust,
or neutral if no clear emotion was present. For
narrative-emotion process, annotators selected one
label from problem, transition, change or filler.
Pairwise comparison task.
In the pairwise com-
parison task, annotators were shown a patient pro-
file, a reference real conversation for that profile
from the Eeyore dataset, and two synthetic conver-
sations generated by different simulators. Annota-
tors were instructed to refer to the real conversation
for the general style and progression of authen-
tic patient communication, not as a strict template.
They should use both the reference conversation
and their clinical judgment to decide which con-
versation more closely reflects how a real patient
would communicate.
Figure 8 shows the task overview, and Figure 9,
10 and 11 illustrates the task interface for the three
annotation steps of each profile. In Step 1, an-
notators read through the patient profile and the
reference real conversation. In Step 2, they re-
viewed two synthetic conversations (only the first
three messages) shown side by side. The therapist
responses were included solely for conversational
context. In Step 3, annotators submitted their pref-
erence and provide a short explanation. Annotators
were encouraged to make a preference whenever
possible, selecting “About Equal” only when no
meaningful difference in realism could be identi-
fied.
Aggregation and ties.
For both tasks, annota-
tions were aggregated within each annotator group
using majority vote. In the pairwise comparison
task, vote ties were rare (3 out of 60 unique pairs)
and were excluded from the majority-vote analy-
sis. In the classification task, ties occurred more
frequently, especially between emotions with sim-

Abstract: Patient simulators are gaining traction in mental health training by providing scalable exposure to complex and sensitive patient interactions. Simulating depressed patients is particularly challenging, as safety constraints and high pa- tient variability complicate simulations and un- derscore the need for simulators that capture diverse and realistic patient behaviors. How- ever, existing evaluations heavily rely on LLM- judges with poorly specified prompts and do not assess behavioral diversity. We introduce PSI-Bench, an automatic evaluation framework that provides interpretable, clinically grounded diagnostics of depression patient simulator be- havior across turn-, dialogue-, and population- level dimensions. Using PSI-Bench, we bench- mark seven LLMs across two simulator frame- works and find that simulators produce overly long, lexically diverse responses, show reduced variability, resolve emotions too quickly, and follow a uniform negative-to-positive trajectory. We also show that the simulation framework has a larger impact on fidelity than the model scale. Results from a human study demonstrate that our benchmark is strongly aligned with expert judgments. Our work reveals key lim- itations of current depression patient simula- tors and provides an interpretable, extensible benchmark to guide future simulator design and evaluation.
